steps.text: Select ripe fruits, preferably those that are locally available and organic.
Chop the fruits into small pieces.
Mix the chopped fruits with brown sugar in a 1:1 ratio by weight.
Place the mixture in a clay pot, plastic jar, or glass jar, leaving some space at the top.
Cover the opening of the jar with a breathable material like a cotton cloth and secure it with a rubber band or thread.
Allow the mixture to ferment in a cool, shaded place for about 7 days.
After fermentation, strain the liquid. This is your FFJ.

track_model.nutrition: Fresh plant material is computed per nutrient from the crop requirement, the candidate tissue midpoint, the tissue part's dry-matter fraction and the nutrient's release fraction. The no-overshoot rule sizes the material to the nutrient that needs the least, so no nutrient exceeds the target fraction; each nutrient's resulting coverage is reported.
track_model.booster: The booster is the source recipe's standard batch at its standard dilution and application rate. Its nutrient amount is reported for information only and does not claim to cover the crop requirement.
track_model.dry_matter: Dry matter is per plant part; the value's corpus source is recorded for each part. Unmapped parts fall back to the herb category.
track_model.release: Release/extraction is per nutrient (N, P, K); the residue-N recovery figure is not reused for P and K.
track_model.dose_rule: no overshoot: the single applied mass is the smallest per-nutrient requirement, so the target fraction is never exceeded; shortfalls are reported as coverage with a top-up note

interpretation.nutrition_track: The nutrition track is a nutrient-equivalence mass: the stated fresh material, spread as chop-and-drop or mulch or brewed as plant tea, would supply the target fraction of the crop's seasonal N/P/K requirement if the dry-matter and release fractions are correct. The mass is sized by the no-overshoot rule to the nutrient that needs the least, so the target is never exceeded and the other nutrients reach only the stated coverage.
interpretation.booster_track: The booster track is the source recipe at its normal strength. It is a small, convenient input, not a way to cover the crop requirement on the stated area.
interpretation.not_a_prescription: The old 'relative signal, not a dose' caveat is replaced by these explicit assumptions. The output is an assumption-bound calculation, not a fertilizer recommendation or a substitute for soil testing.

limitations: Dry matter is per plant part but every value is a corpus point estimate; bark uses a wood-moisture proxy and flower uses whole-plant water content.
P release uses a plant-uptake efficiency (less than 20%) as a conservative proxy because the corpus has no direct residue-P release measurement.
K release of 0.80 follows 'most of the potassium is leached' rather than a measured fraction.
The plant-tea steep ratio (10 L water per kg fresh material) is a method convention; only the 1:10 finished-tea dilution and the application rate are corpus-sourced.
The ferment density is a water-density unit convention, not a measured extract density.
The model does not account for soil nutrient supply, leaching, volatilization, fixation, plant uptake efficiency, or nutrient interactions.
WSP uses the source recipe's bone/vinegar steps; the candidate plant material is a derived substitution, not a source recipe.
The crop requirement unit (kg/ha) is confirmed by the owner (2026-10-18) even though Crop_Requirements.json does not state it.
The no-overshoot sizing keeps the target fraction from being exceeded, so nutrients that are not the sizing nutrient are deliberately under-supplied; their coverage and top-up note are reported.

The implied mulch depth approximates the fresh material's loose volume with the approved plant-tea water-to-material convention (10 L water per kg material), an upper bound on the material volume, so the depth check is conservative.

interpretation.nutrition_track: The nutrition track is a nutrient-equivalence mass: the stated fresh material, spread as chop-and-drop or mulch or brewed as plant tea, would supply the target fraction of the crop's seasonal N/P/K requirement if the dry-matter and release fractions are correct. The mass is sized by the no-overshoot rule to the nutrient that needs the least, so the target is never exceeded and the other nutrients reach only the stated coverage.
interpretation.booster_track: The booster track is the source recipe at its normal strength. It is a small, convenient input, not a way to cover the crop requirement on the stated area.
interpretation.not_a_prescription: The old 'relative signal, not a dose' caveat is replaced by these explicit assumptions. The output is an assumption-bound calculation, not a fertilizer recommendation or a substitute for soil testing.

limitations: Dry matter is per plant part but every value is a corpus point estimate; bark uses a wood-moisture proxy and flower uses whole-plant water content.
P release uses a plant-uptake efficiency (less than 20%) as a conservative proxy because the corpus has no direct residue-P release measurement.
K release of 0.80 follows 'most of the potassium is leached' rather than a measured fraction.
The plant-tea steep ratio (10 L water per kg fresh material) is a method convention; only the 1:10 finished-tea dilution and the application rate are corpus-sourced.
The ferment density is a water-density unit convention, not a measured extract density.
The model does not account for soil nutrient supply, leaching, volatilization, fixation, plant uptake efficiency, or nutrient interactions.
WSP uses the source recipe's bone/vinegar steps; the candidate plant material is a derived substitution, not a source recipe.
The crop requirement unit (kg/ha) is confirmed by the owner (2026-10-18) even though Crop_Requirements.json does not state it.
The no-overshoot sizing keeps the target fraction from being exceeded, so nutrients that are not the sizing nutrient are deliberately under-supplied; their coverage and top-up note are reported.

The implied mulch depth approximates the fresh material's loose volume with the approved plant-tea water-to-material convention (10 L water per kg material), an upper bound on the material volume, so the depth check is conservative.

steps.text: Collect the young shoots of plants early in the morning when the dew is still present.
Chop the shoots into small pieces.
Mix the chopped shoots with brown sugar in a 1:1 ratio by weight.
Place the mixture in a clay pot, plastic jar, or glass jar, leaving some space at the top.
Cover the opening of the jar with a breathable material like a cotton cloth and secure it with a rubber band or thread.
Allow the mixture to ferment in a cool, shaded place for about 7 days.
After fermentation, strain the liquid. This is your FPJ.

interpretation.nutrition_track: The nutrition track is a nutrient-equivalence mass: the stated fresh material, spread as chop-and-drop or mulch or brewed as plant tea, would supply the target fraction of the crop's seasonal N/P/K requirement if the dry-matter and release fractions are correct. The mass is sized by the no-overshoot rule to the nutrient that needs the least, so the target is never exceeded and the other nutrients reach only the stated coverage.
interpretation.booster_track: The booster track is the source recipe at its normal strength. It is a small, convenient input, not a way to cover the crop requirement on the stated area.
interpretation.not_a_prescription: The old 'relative signal, not a dose' caveat is replaced by these explicit assumptions. The output is an assumption-bound calculation, not a fertilizer recommendation or a substitute for soil testing.

limitations: Dry matter is per plant part but every value is a corpus point estimate; bark uses a wood-moisture proxy and flower uses whole-plant water content.
P release uses a plant-uptake efficiency (less than 20%) as a conservative proxy because the corpus has no direct residue-P release measurement.
K release of 0.80 follows 'most of the potassium is leached' rather than a measured fraction.
The plant-tea steep ratio (10 L water per kg fresh material) is a method convention; only the 1:10 finished-tea dilution and the application rate are corpus-sourced.
The ferment density is a water-density unit convention, not a measured extract density.
The model does not account for soil nutrient supply, leaching, volatilization, fixation, plant uptake efficiency, or nutrient interactions.
WSP uses the source recipe's bone/vinegar steps; the candidate plant material is a derived substitution, not a source recipe.
The crop requirement unit (kg/ha) is confirmed by the owner (2026-10-18) even though Crop_Requirements.json does not state it.
The no-overshoot sizing keeps the target fraction from being exceeded, so nutrients that are not the sizing nutrient are deliberately under-supplied; their coverage and top-up note are reported.

The implied mulch depth approximates the fresh material's loose volume with the approved plant-tea water-to-material convention (10 L water per kg material), an upper bound on the material volume, so the depth check is conservative.

interpretation.nutrition_track: The nutrition track is a nutrient-equivalence mass: the stated fresh material, spread as chop-and-drop or mulch or brewed as plant tea, would supply the target fraction of the crop's seasonal N/P/K requirement if the dry-matter and release fractions are correct. The mass is sized by the no-overshoot rule to the nutrient that needs the least, so the target is never exceeded and the other nutrients reach only the stated coverage.
interpretation.booster_track: The booster track is the source recipe at its normal strength. It is a small, convenient input, not a way to cover the crop requirement on the stated area.
interpretation.not_a_prescription: The old 'relative signal, not a dose' caveat is replaced by these explicit assumptions. The output is an assumption-bound calculation, not a fertilizer recommendation or a substitute for soil testing.

limitations: Dry matter is per plant part but every value is a corpus point estimate; bark uses a wood-moisture proxy and flower uses whole-plant water content.
P release uses a plant-uptake efficiency (less than 20%) as a conservative proxy because the corpus has no direct residue-P release measurement.
K release of 0.80 follows 'most of the potassium is leached' rather than a measured fraction.
The plant-tea steep ratio (10 L water per kg fresh material) is a method convention; only the 1:10 finished-tea dilution and the application rate are corpus-sourced.
The ferment density is a water-density unit convention, not a measured extract density.
The model does not account for soil nutrient supply, leaching, volatilization, fixation, plant uptake efficiency, or nutrient interactions.
WSP uses the source recipe's bone/vinegar steps; the candidate plant material is a derived substitution, not a source recipe.
The crop requirement unit (kg/ha) is confirmed by the owner (2026-10-18) even though Crop_Requirements.json does not state it.
The no-overshoot sizing keeps the target fraction from being exceeded, so nutrients that are not the sizing nutrient are deliberately under-supplied; their coverage and top-up note are reported.

The implied mulch depth approximates the fresh material's loose volume with the approved plant-tea water-to-material convention (10 L water per kg material), an upper bound on the material volume, so the depth check is conservative.

interpretation.nutrition_track: The nutrition track is a nutrient-equivalence mass: the stated fresh material, spread as chop-and-drop or mulch or brewed as plant tea, would supply the target fraction of the crop's seasonal N/P/K requirement if the dry-matter and release fractions are correct. The mass is sized by the no-overshoot rule to the nutrient that needs the least, so the target is never exceeded and the other nutrients reach only the stated coverage.
interpretation.booster_track: The booster track is the source recipe at its normal strength. It is a small, convenient input, not a way to cover the crop requirement on the stated area.
interpretation.not_a_prescription: The old 'relative signal, not a dose' caveat is replaced by these explicit assumptions. The output is an assumption-bound calculation, not a fertilizer recommendation or a substitute for soil testing.

limitations: Dry matter is per plant part but every value is a corpus point estimate; bark uses a wood-moisture proxy and flower uses whole-plant water content.
P release uses a plant-uptake efficiency (less than 20%) as a conservative proxy because the corpus has no direct residue-P release measurement.
K release of 0.80 follows 'most of the potassium is leached' rather than a measured fraction.
The plant-tea steep ratio (10 L water per kg fresh material) is a method convention; only the 1:10 finished-tea dilution and the application rate are corpus-sourced.
The ferment density is a water-density unit convention, not a measured extract density.
The model does not account for soil nutrient supply, leaching, volatilization, fixation, plant uptake efficiency, or nutrient interactions.
WSP uses the source recipe's bone/vinegar steps; the candidate plant material is a derived substitution, not a source recipe.
The crop requirement unit (kg/ha) is confirmed by the owner (2026-10-18) even though Crop_Requirements.json does not state it.
The no-overshoot sizing keeps the target fraction from being exceeded, so nutrients that are not the sizing nutrient are deliberately under-supplied; their coverage and top-up note are reported.

The implied mulch depth approximates the fresh material's loose volume with the approved plant-tea water-to-material convention (10 L water per kg material), an upper bound on the material volume, so the depth check is conservative.

ingredients: Bones (fish bones or small animal bones)

steps.text: Clean the bones thoroughly and dry them in the sun.
Once dry, crush the bones into small pieces.
Place the crushed bones in a jar and add vinegar until the bones are fully submerged.
Cover the jar with a breathable material and secure it with a rubber band or thread.
Allow the mixture to sit in a cool, shaded place for about 10 days, or until the bubbling stops.
Strain the liquid. This is your WSP.

interpretation.nutrition_track: The nutrition track is a nutrient-equivalence mass: the stated fresh material, spread as chop-and-drop or mulch or brewed as plant tea, would supply the target fraction of the crop's seasonal N/P/K requirement if the dry-matter and release fractions are correct. The mass is sized by the no-overshoot rule to the nutrient that needs the least, so the target is never exceeded and the other nutrients reach only the stated coverage.
interpretation.booster_track: The booster track is the source recipe at its normal strength. It is a small, convenient input, not a way to cover the crop requirement on the stated area.
interpretation.not_a_prescription: The old 'relative signal, not a dose' caveat is replaced by these explicit assumptions. The output is an assumption-bound calculation, not a fertilizer recommendation or a substitute for soil testing.

limitations: Dry matter is per plant part but every value is a corpus point estimate; bark uses a wood-moisture proxy and flower uses whole-plant water content.
P release uses a plant-uptake efficiency (less than 20%) as a conservative proxy because the corpus has no direct residue-P release measurement.
K release of 0.80 follows 'most of the potassium is leached' rather than a measured fraction.
The plant-tea steep ratio (10 L water per kg fresh material) is a method convention; only the 1:10 finished-tea dilution and the application rate are corpus-sourced.
The ferment density is a water-density unit convention, not a measured extract density.
The model does not account for soil nutrient supply, leaching, volatilization, fixation, plant uptake efficiency, or nutrient interactions.
WSP uses the source recipe's bone/vinegar steps; the candidate plant material is a derived substitution, not a source recipe.
The crop requirement unit (kg/ha) is confirmed by the owner (2026-10-18) even though Crop_Requirements.json does not state it.
The no-overshoot sizing keeps the target fraction from being exceeded, so nutrients that are not the sizing nutrient are deliberately under-supplied; their coverage and top-up note are reported.

The implied mulch depth approximates the fresh material's loose volume with the approved plant-tea water-to-material convention (10 L water per kg material), an upper bound on the material volume, so the depth check is conservative.

track_model.dose_rule: no overshoot: the single applied mass is the smallest per-nutrient requirement, so the target fraction is never exceeded; shortfalls are reported as coverage with a top-up note

interpretation.nutrition_track: The nutrition track is a nutrient-equivalence mass: the stated fresh material, spread as chop-and-drop or mulch or brewed as plant tea, would supply the target fraction of the crop's seasonal N/P/K requirement if the dry-matter and release fractions are correct. The mass is sized by the no-overshoot rule to the nutrient that needs the least, so the target is never exceeded and the other nutrients reach only the stated coverage.
interpretation.booster_track: The booster track is the source recipe at its normal strength. It is a small, convenient input, not a way to cover the crop requirement on the stated area.
interpretation.not_a_prescription: The old 'relative signal, not a dose' caveat is replaced by these explicit assumptions. The output is an assumption-bound calculation, not a fertilizer recommendation or a substitute for soil testing.

limitations: Dry matter is per plant part but every value is a corpus point estimate; bark uses a wood-moisture proxy and flower uses whole-plant water content.
P release uses a plant-uptake efficiency (less than 20%) as a conservative proxy because the corpus has no direct residue-P release measurement.
K release of 0.80 follows 'most of the potassium is leached' rather than a measured fraction.
The plant-tea steep ratio (10 L water per kg fresh material) is a method convention; only the 1:10 finished-tea dilution and the application rate are corpus-sourced.
The ferment density is a water-density unit convention, not a measured extract density.
The model does not account for soil nutrient supply, leaching, volatilization, fixation, plant uptake efficiency, or nutrient interactions.
WSP uses the source recipe's bone/vinegar steps; the candidate plant material is a derived substitution, not a source recipe.
The crop requirement unit (kg/ha) is confirmed by the owner (2026-10-18) even though Crop_Requirements.json does not state it.
The no-overshoot sizing keeps the target fraction from being exceeded, so nutrients that are not the sizing nutrient are deliberately under-supplied; their coverage and top-up note are reported.

The implied mulch depth approximates the fresh material's loose volume with the approved plant-tea water-to-material convention (10 L water per kg material), an upper bound on the material volume, so the depth check is conservative.

steps.text: Collect the young shoots of plants early in the morning when the dew is still present.
Chop the shoots into small pieces.
Mix the chopped shoots with brown sugar in a 1:1 ratio by weight.
Place the mixture in a clay pot, plastic jar, or glass jar, leaving some space at the top.
Cover the opening of the jar with a breathable material like a cotton cloth and secure it with a rubber band or thread.
Allow the mixture to ferment in a cool, shaded place for about 7 days.
After fermentation, strain the liquid. This is your FPJ.

interpretation.nutrition_track: The nutrition track is a nutrient-equivalence mass: the stated fresh material, spread as chop-and-drop or mulch or brewed as plant tea, would supply the target fraction of the crop's seasonal N/P/K requirement if the dry-matter and release fractions are correct. The mass is sized by the no-overshoot rule to the nutrient that needs the least, so the target is never exceeded and the other nutrients reach only the stated coverage.
interpretation.booster_track: The booster track is the source recipe at its normal strength. It is a small, convenient input, not a way to cover the crop requirement on the stated area.
interpretation.not_a_prescription: The old 'relative signal, not a dose' caveat is replaced by these explicit assumptions. The output is an assumption-bound calculation, not a fertilizer recommendation or a substitute for soil testing.

limitations: Dry matter is per plant part but every value is a corpus point estimate; bark uses a wood-moisture proxy and flower uses whole-plant water content.
P release uses a plant-uptake efficiency (less than 20%) as a conservative proxy because the corpus has no direct residue-P release measurement.
K release of 0.80 follows 'most of the potassium is leached' rather than a measured fraction.
The plant-tea steep ratio (10 L water per kg fresh material) is a method convention; only the 1:10 finished-tea dilution and the application rate are corpus-sourced.
The ferment density is a water-density unit convention, not a measured extract density.
The model does not account for soil nutrient supply, leaching, volatilization, fixation, plant uptake efficiency, or nutrient interactions.
WSP uses the source recipe's bone/vinegar steps; the candidate plant material is a derived substitution, not a source recipe.
The crop requirement unit (kg/ha) is confirmed by the owner (2026-10-18) even though Crop_Requirements.json does not state it.
The no-overshoot sizing keeps the target fraction from being exceeded, so nutrients that are not the sizing nutrient are deliberately under-supplied; their coverage and top-up note are reported.

The implied mulch depth approximates the fresh material's loose volume with the approved plant-tea water-to-material convention (10 L water per kg material), an upper bound on the material volume, so the depth check is conservative.

steps.text: Select ripe fruits, preferably those that are locally available and organic.
Chop the fruits into small pieces.
Mix the chopped fruits with brown sugar in a 1:1 ratio by weight.
Place the mixture in a clay pot, plastic jar, or glass jar, leaving some space at the top.
Cover the opening of the jar with a breathable material like a cotton cloth and secure it with a rubber band or thread.
Allow the mixture to ferment in a cool, shaded place for about 7 days.
After fermentation, strain the liquid. This is your FFJ.

nutrient_scope.nitrogen: N is included by the 2026-10-17 owner decision; the old 'nitrogen is never comparable' rule is replaced by these assumptions.

crop_requirement.unit_note: kg/ha is CONFIRMED by the owner (2026-10-18); the file does not state a unit, but the values and the corpus convention are kg/ha.
crop_requirement.midpoint: arithmetic mean of the declared range
crop_requirement.basis: full seasonal crop requirement, not a deficit after soil supply

tissue_basis.selection: highest complete min/max midpoint among the profile's parts for each nutrient; a recipe-named part is preferred for that recipe's target nutrient when it has complete data
tissue_basis.incomplete_values: a value with only min or only max is ignored

dry_matter_fraction.unit: kg dry matter per kg fresh plant material

source.quote: Assuming a medium leaf weight of 2 g fresh weight and a leaf water content of 85%.
source.derivation: 1 - 0.85 = 0.15 kg dry matter per kg fresh leaf; other parts use their own quote below.

dry_matter_fraction.caveat: Each part value is a corpus-derived point estimate, not a measurement of the specific candidate. Bark uses a wood-moisture proxy and flower uses the whole-plant water content because the corpus has no separate measurement.

nutrient_release_fraction.unit: kg plant-available nutrient per kg tissue nutrient

source.quote: In 1943, Norman and Werkman labeled soybeans with 15N. Addition of the labeled residue to soil showed that 26% of the tagged N was recovered by a subsequent crop.
source.derivation: N keeps the 0.26 labeled-residue recovery. P and K use separate sources below and do not reuse this N figure.

nutrient_release_fraction.caveat: N and K have residue/litter evidence; P uses a plant-uptake efficiency as a conservative proxy. All three are approved by the owner (2026-10-18).

sugar_to_plant_material_ratio.unit: kg brown sugar per kg fresh plant material

source.quote: Mix the ingredients with brown sugar in a 1:1 ratio for storage.

sugar_to_plant_material_ratio.caveat: The KNF text also allows 1/2 to 2/3 sugar by weight for immediate use; v2 follows the app recipes' 1:1 storage ratio.

source.quote: Put the bones in the jar with BRV (charcoal: BRV= 1:10).

vinegar_to_material_ratio.caveat: The corpus ratio is for bone charcoal in brown rice vinegar. The app's WSP uses bones plus vinegar and says 'until submerged'; v2 uses the WSP/WCP 1:10 ratio. The plant-material substitution is a derived proposal, not a source recipe.

source.quote: Water-density approximation used to convert a plant/sugar or plant/vinegar mixture to litres.

ferment_density_kg_per_l.caveat: Sugar solutions and plant extracts are denser than water; v2 treats 1 kg as 1 L so the dilution arithmetic is transparent. This is a unit convention, not a corpus-derived dosing constant.

mulch_depth_cm.caveat: The 5 cm maximum is for grass clippings; coarser or drier materials can be applied deeper (the corpus also describes 8-12 inch sheet mulch). v2 reports it as the default fresh-material mulch depth.

track_model.nutrition: Fresh plant material is computed per nutrient from the crop requirement, the candidate tissue midpoint, the tissue part's dry-matter fraction and the nutrient's release fraction. The no-overshoot rule sizes the material to the nutrient that needs the least, so no nutrient exceeds the target fraction; each nutrient's resulting coverage is reported.
track_model.booster: The booster is the source recipe's standard batch at its standard dilution and application rate. Its nutrient amount is reported for information only and does not claim to cover the crop requirement.
track_model.dry_matter: Dry matter is per plant part; the value's corpus source is recorded for each part. Unmapped parts fall back to the herb category.
track_model.release: Release/extraction is per nutrient (N, P, K); the residue-N recovery figure is not reused for P and K.
track_model.dose_rule: no overshoot: the single applied mass is the smallest per-nutrient requirement, so the target fraction is never exceeded; shortfalls are reported as coverage with a top-up note

interpretation.nutrition_track: The nutrition track is a nutrient-equivalence mass: the stated fresh material, spread as chop-and-drop or mulch or brewed as plant tea, would supply the target fraction of the crop's seasonal N/P/K requirement if the dry-matter and release fractions are correct. The mass is sized by the no-overshoot rule to the nutrient that needs the least, so the target is never exceeded and the other nutrients reach only the stated coverage.
interpretation.booster_track: The booster track is the source recipe at its normal strength. It is a small, convenient input, not a way to cover the crop requirement on the stated area.
interpretation.not_a_prescription: The old 'relative signal, not a dose' caveat is replaced by these explicit assumptions. The output is an assumption-bound calculation, not a fertilizer recommendation or a substitute for soil testing.

limitations: Dry matter is per plant part but every value is a corpus point estimate; bark uses a wood-moisture proxy and flower uses whole-plant water content.
P release uses a plant-uptake efficiency (less than 20%) as a conservative proxy because the corpus has no direct residue-P release measurement.
K release of 0.80 follows 'most of the potassium is leached' rather than a measured fraction.
The plant-tea steep ratio (10 L water per kg fresh material) is a method convention; only the 1:10 finished-tea dilution and the application rate are corpus-sourced.
The ferment density is a water-density unit convention, not a measured extract density.
The model does not account for soil nutrient supply, leaching, volatilization, fixation, plant uptake efficiency, or nutrient interactions.
WSP uses the source recipe's bone/vinegar steps; the candidate plant material is a derived substitution, not a source recipe.
The crop requirement unit (kg/ha) is confirmed by the owner (2026-10-18) even though Crop_Requirements.json does not state it.
The no-overshoot sizing keeps the target fraction from being exceeded, so nutrients that are not the sizing nutrient are deliberately under-supplied; their coverage and top-up note are reported.

The implied mulch depth approximates the fresh material's loose volume with the approved plant-tea water-to-material convention (10 L water per kg material), an upper bound on the material volume, so the depth check is conservative.

track_model.nutrition: Fresh plant material is computed per nutrient from the crop requirement, the candidate tissue midpoint, the tissue part's dry-matter fraction and the nutrient's release fraction. The no-overshoot rule sizes the material to the nutrient that needs the least, so no nutrient exceeds the target fraction; each nutrient's resulting coverage is reported.
track_model.booster: The booster is the source recipe's standard batch at its standard dilution and application rate. Its nutrient amount is reported for information only and does not claim to cover the crop requirement.
track_model.dry_matter: Dry matter is per plant part; the value's corpus source is recorded for each part. Unmapped parts fall back to the herb category.
track_model.release: Release/extraction is per nutrient (N, P, K); the residue-N recovery figure is not reused for P and K.
track_model.dose_rule: no overshoot: the single applied mass is the smallest per-nutrient requirement, so the target fraction is never exceeded; shortfalls are reported as coverage with a top-up note

interpretation.nutrition_track: The nutrition track is a nutrient-equivalence mass: the stated fresh material, spread as chop-and-drop or mulch or brewed as plant tea, would supply the target fraction of the crop's seasonal N/P/K requirement if the dry-matter and release fractions are correct. The mass is sized by the no-overshoot rule to the nutrient that needs the least, so the target is never exceeded and the other nutrients reach only the stated coverage.
interpretation.booster_track: The booster track is the source recipe at its normal strength. It is a small, convenient input, not a way to cover the crop requirement on the stated area.
interpretation.not_a_prescription: The old 'relative signal, not a dose' caveat is replaced by these explicit assumptions. The output is an assumption-bound calculation, not a fertilizer recommendation or a substitute for soil testing.

limitations: Dry matter is per plant part but every value is a corpus point estimate; bark uses a wood-moisture proxy and flower uses whole-plant water content.
P release uses a plant-uptake efficiency (less than 20%) as a conservative proxy because the corpus has no direct residue-P release measurement.
K release of 0.80 follows 'most of the potassium is leached' rather than a measured fraction.
The plant-tea steep ratio (10 L water per kg fresh material) is a method convention; only the 1:10 finished-tea dilution and the application rate are corpus-sourced.
The ferment density is a water-density unit convention, not a measured extract density.
The model does not account for soil nutrient supply, leaching, volatilization, fixation, plant uptake efficiency, or nutrient interactions.
WSP uses the source recipe's bone/vinegar steps; the candidate plant material is a derived substitution, not a source recipe.
The crop requirement unit (kg/ha) is confirmed by the owner (2026-10-18) even though Crop_Requirements.json does not state it.
The no-overshoot sizing keeps the target fraction from being exceeded, so nutrients that are not the sizing nutrient are deliberately under-supplied; their coverage and top-up note are reported.

The implied mulch depth approximates the fresh material's loose volume with the approved plant-tea water-to-material convention (10 L water per kg material), an upper bound on the material volume, so the depth check is conservative.

assumptions: Fresh plant material is computed per nutrient from the crop requirement midpoint, the candidate tissue midpoint, the tissue part's dry-matter fraction and the nutrient's release fraction.

steps.text: Select ripe fruits, preferably those that are locally available and organic.
Chop the fruits into small pieces.
Mix the chopped fruits with brown sugar in a 1:1 ratio by weight.
Place the mixture in a clay pot, plastic jar, or glass jar, leaving some space at the top.
Cover the opening of the jar with a breathable material like a cotton cloth and secure it with a rubber band or thread.
Allow the mixture to ferment in a cool, shaded place for about 7 days.
After fermentation, strain the liquid. This is your FFJ.

nutrient_scope.nitrogen: N is included by the 2026-10-17 owner decision; the old 'nitrogen is never comparable' rule is replaced by these assumptions.
nutrient_scope.calcium: Ca is out of scope for v2 because Crop_Requirements.json has no crop Ca requirement; WCA is not computable.

crop_requirement.midpoint: arithmetic mean of the declared range
crop_requirement.basis: full seasonal crop requirement, not a deficit after soil supply

tissue_basis.selection: highest complete min/max midpoint among the profile's parts for each nutrient; a recipe-named part is preferred for that recipe's target nutrient when it has complete data
tissue_basis.incomplete_values: a value with only min or only max is ignored

dry_matter_fraction.unit: kg dry matter per kg fresh plant material

source.quote: Assuming a medium leaf weight of 2 g fresh weight and a leaf water content of 85%.
source.derivation: 1 - 0.85 = 0.15 kg dry matter per kg fresh leaf; other parts use their own quote below.

dry_matter_fraction.caveat: Each part value is a corpus-derived point estimate, not a measurement of the specific candidate. Bark uses a wood-moisture proxy and flower uses the whole-plant water content because the corpus has no separate measurement.

nutrient_release_fraction.unit: kg plant-available nutrient per kg tissue nutrient

source.quote: In 1943, Norman and Werkman labeled soybeans with 15N. Addition of the labeled residue to soil showed that 26% of the tagged N was recovered by a subsequent crop.
source.derivation: N keeps the 0.26 labeled-residue recovery. P and K use separate sources below and do not reuse this N figure.

nutrient_release_fraction.caveat: N and K have residue/litter evidence; P uses a plant-uptake efficiency as a conservative proxy. All three are approved by the owner (2026-10-18).

sugar_to_plant_material_ratio.unit: kg brown sugar per kg fresh plant material

source.quote: Mix the ingredients with brown sugar in a 1:1 ratio for storage.

sugar_to_plant_material_ratio.caveat: The KNF text also allows 1/2 to 2/3 sugar by weight for immediate use; v2 follows the app recipes' 1:1 storage ratio.

source.quote: Put the bones in the jar with BRV (charcoal: BRV= 1:10).

vinegar_to_material_ratio.caveat: The corpus ratio is for bone charcoal in brown rice vinegar. The app's WSP uses bones plus vinegar and says 'until submerged'; v2 uses the WSP/WCP 1:10 ratio. The plant-material substitution is a derived proposal, not a source recipe.

source.quote: Water-density approximation used to convert a plant/sugar or plant/vinegar mixture to litres.

ferment_density_kg_per_l.caveat: Sugar solutions and plant extracts are denser than water; v2 treats 1 kg as 1 L so the dilution arithmetic is transparent. This is a unit convention, not a corpus-derived dosing constant.

steps.text: Clean the bones thoroughly and dry them in the sun.

Place the crushed bones in a jar and add vinegar until the bones are fully submerged.

Strain the liquid. This is your WSP.

ingredients: Bones (fish bones or small animal bones)

steps.text: Clean the bones thoroughly and dry them in the sun.
Once dry, crush the bones into small pieces.
Place the crushed bones in a jar and add vinegar until the bones are fully submerged.
Cover the jar with a breathable material and secure it with a rubber band or thread.
Allow the mixture to sit in a cool, shaded place for about 10 days, or until the bubbling stops.
Strain the liquid. This is your WSP.

interpretation.nutrition_track: The nutrition track is a nutrient-equivalence mass: the stated fresh material, spread as chop-and-drop or mulch or brewed as plant tea, would supply the target fraction of the crop's seasonal N/P/K requirement if the dry-matter and release fractions are correct. The mass is sized by the no-overshoot rule to the nutrient that needs the least, so the target is never exceeded and the other nutrients reach only the stated coverage.
interpretation.booster_track: The booster track is the source recipe at its normal strength. It is a small, convenient input, not a way to cover the crop requirement on the stated area.
interpretation.not_a_prescription: The old 'relative signal, not a dose' caveat is replaced by these explicit assumptions. The output is an assumption-bound calculation, not a fertilizer recommendation or a substitute for soil testing.

limitations: Dry matter is per plant part but every value is a corpus point estimate; bark uses a wood-moisture proxy and flower uses whole-plant water content.
P release uses a plant-uptake efficiency (less than 20%) as a conservative proxy because the corpus has no direct residue-P release measurement.
K release of 0.80 follows 'most of the potassium is leached' rather than a measured fraction.
The plant-tea steep ratio (10 L water per kg fresh material) is a method convention; only the 1:10 finished-tea dilution and the application rate are corpus-sourced.
The ferment density is a water-density unit convention, not a measured extract density.
The model does not account for soil nutrient supply, leaching, volatilization, fixation, plant uptake efficiency, or nutrient interactions.
WSP uses the source recipe's bone/vinegar steps; the candidate plant material is a derived substitution, not a source recipe.
The crop requirement unit (kg/ha) is confirmed by the owner (2026-10-18) even though Crop_Requirements.json does not state it.
The no-overshoot sizing keeps the target fraction from being exceeded, so nutrients that are not the sizing nutrient are deliberately under-supplied; their coverage and top-up note are reported.

The implied mulch depth approximates the fresh material's loose volume with the approved plant-tea water-to-material convention (10 L water per kg material), an upper bound on the material volume, so the depth check is conservative.

interpretation.nutrition_track: The nutrition track is a nutrient-equivalence mass: the stated fresh material, spread as chop-and-drop or mulch or brewed as plant tea, would supply the target fraction of the crop's seasonal N/P/K requirement if the dry-matter and release fractions are correct. The mass is sized by the no-overshoot rule to the nutrient that needs the least, so the target is never exceeded and the other nutrients reach only the stated coverage.
interpretation.booster_track: The booster track is the source recipe at its normal strength. It is a small, convenient input, not a way to cover the crop requirement on the stated area.
interpretation.not_a_prescription: The old 'relative signal, not a dose' caveat is replaced by these explicit assumptions. The output is an assumption-bound calculation, not a fertilizer recommendation or a substitute for soil testing.

limitations: Dry matter is per plant part but every value is a corpus point estimate; bark uses a wood-moisture proxy and flower uses whole-plant water content.
P release uses a plant-uptake efficiency (less than 20%) as a conservative proxy because the corpus has no direct residue-P release measurement.
K release of 0.80 follows 'most of the potassium is leached' rather than a measured fraction.
The plant-tea steep ratio (10 L water per kg fresh material) is a method convention; only the 1:10 finished-tea dilution and the application rate are corpus-sourced.
The ferment density is a water-density unit convention, not a measured extract density.
The model does not account for soil nutrient supply, leaching, volatilization, fixation, plant uptake efficiency, or nutrient interactions.
WSP uses the source recipe's bone/vinegar steps; the candidate plant material is a derived substitution, not a source recipe.
The crop requirement unit (kg/ha) is confirmed by the owner (2026-10-18) even though Crop_Requirements.json does not state it.
The no-overshoot sizing keeps the target fraction from being exceeded, so nutrients that are not the sizing nutrient are deliberately under-supplied; their coverage and top-up note are reported.

The implied mulch depth approximates the fresh material's loose volume with the approved plant-tea water-to-material convention (10 L water per kg material), an upper bound on the material volume, so the depth check is conservative.

steps.text: Collect the young shoots of plants early in the morning when the dew is still present.
Chop the shoots into small pieces.
Mix the chopped shoots with brown sugar in a 1:1 ratio by weight.
Place the mixture in a clay pot, plastic jar, or glass jar, leaving some space at the top.
Cover the opening of the jar with a breathable material like a cotton cloth and secure it with a rubber band or thread.
Allow the mixture to ferment in a cool, shaded place for about 7 days.
After fermentation, strain the liquid. This is your FPJ.

steps.text: Select ripe fruits, preferably those that are locally available and organic.
Chop the fruits into small pieces.
Mix the chopped fruits with brown sugar in a 1:1 ratio by weight.
Place the mixture in a clay pot, plastic jar, or glass jar, leaving some space at the top.
Cover the opening of the jar with a breathable material like a cotton cloth and secure it with a rubber band or thread.
Allow the mixture to ferment in a cool, shaded place for about 7 days.
After fermentation, strain the liquid. This is your FFJ.

track_model.nutrition: Fresh plant material is computed per nutrient from the crop requirement, the candidate tissue midpoint, the tissue part's dry-matter fraction and the nutrient's release fraction. The no-overshoot rule sizes the material to the nutrient that needs the least, so no nutrient exceeds the target fraction; each nutrient's resulting coverage is reported.
track_model.booster: The booster is the source recipe's standard batch at its standard dilution and application rate. Its nutrient amount is reported for information only and does not claim to cover the crop requirement.
track_model.dry_matter: Dry matter is per plant part; the value's corpus source is recorded for each part. Unmapped parts fall back to the herb category.
track_model.release: Release/extraction is per nutrient (N, P, K); the residue-N recovery figure is not reused for P and K.
track_model.dose_rule: no overshoot: the single applied mass is the smallest per-nutrient requirement, so the target fraction is never exceeded; shortfalls are reported as coverage with a top-up note

interpretation.nutrition_track: The nutrition track is a nutrient-equivalence mass: the stated fresh material, spread as chop-and-drop or mulch or brewed as plant tea, would supply the target fraction of the crop's seasonal N/P/K requirement if the dry-matter and release fractions are correct. The mass is sized by the no-overshoot rule to the nutrient that needs the least, so the target is never exceeded and the other nutrients reach only the stated coverage.
interpretation.booster_track: The booster track is the source recipe at its normal strength. It is a small, convenient input, not a way to cover the crop requirement on the stated area.
interpretation.not_a_prescription: The old 'relative signal, not a dose' caveat is replaced by these explicit assumptions. The output is an assumption-bound calculation, not a fertilizer recommendation or a substitute for soil testing.

limitations: Dry matter is per plant part but every value is a corpus point estimate; bark uses a wood-moisture proxy and flower uses whole-plant water content.
P release uses a plant-uptake efficiency (less than 20%) as a conservative proxy because the corpus has no direct residue-P release measurement.
K release of 0.80 follows 'most of the potassium is leached' rather than a measured fraction.
The plant-tea steep ratio (10 L water per kg fresh material) is a method convention; only the 1:10 finished-tea dilution and the application rate are corpus-sourced.
The ferment density is a water-density unit convention, not a measured extract density.
The model does not account for soil nutrient supply, leaching, volatilization, fixation, plant uptake efficiency, or nutrient interactions.
WSP uses the source recipe's bone/vinegar steps; the candidate plant material is a derived substitution, not a source recipe.
The crop requirement unit (kg/ha) is confirmed by the owner (2026-10-18) even though Crop_Requirements.json does not state it.
The no-overshoot sizing keeps the target fraction from being exceeded, so nutrients that are not the sizing nutrient are deliberately under-supplied; their coverage and top-up note are reported.

The implied mulch depth approximates the fresh material's loose volume with the approved plant-tea water-to-material convention (10 L water per kg material), an upper bound on the material volume, so the depth check is conservative.

track_model.nutrition: Fresh plant material is computed per nutrient from the crop requirement, the candidate tissue midpoint, the tissue part's dry-matter fraction and the nutrient's release fraction. The no-overshoot rule sizes the material to the nutrient that needs the least, so no nutrient exceeds the target fraction; each nutrient's resulting coverage is reported.
track_model.booster: The booster is the source recipe's standard batch at its standard dilution and application rate. Its nutrient amount is reported for information only and does not claim to cover the crop requirement.
track_model.dry_matter: Dry matter is per plant part; the value's corpus source is recorded for each part. Unmapped parts fall back to the herb category.
track_model.release: Release/extraction is per nutrient (N, P, K); the residue-N recovery figure is not reused for P and K.
track_model.dose_rule: no overshoot: the single applied mass is the smallest per-nutrient requirement, so the target fraction is never exceeded; shortfalls are reported as coverage with a top-up note

interpretation.nutrition_track: The nutrition track is a nutrient-equivalence mass: the stated fresh material, spread as chop-and-drop or mulch or brewed as plant tea, would supply the target fraction of the crop's seasonal N/P/K requirement if the dry-matter and release fractions are correct. The mass is sized by the no-overshoot rule to the nutrient that needs the least, so the target is never exceeded and the other nutrients reach only the stated coverage.
interpretation.booster_track: The booster track is the source recipe at its normal strength. It is a small, convenient input, not a way to cover the crop requirement on the stated area.
interpretation.not_a_prescription: The old 'relative signal, not a dose' caveat is replaced by these explicit assumptions. The output is an assumption-bound calculation, not a fertilizer recommendation or a substitute for soil testing.

limitations: Dry matter is per plant part but every value is a corpus point estimate; bark uses a wood-moisture proxy and flower uses whole-plant water content.
P release uses a plant-uptake efficiency (less than 20%) as a conservative proxy because the corpus has no direct residue-P release measurement.
K release of 0.80 follows 'most of the potassium is leached' rather than a measured fraction.
The plant-tea steep ratio (10 L water per kg fresh material) is a method convention; only the 1:10 finished-tea dilution and the application rate are corpus-sourced.
The ferment density is a water-density unit convention, not a measured extract density.
The model does not account for soil nutrient supply, leaching, volatilization, fixation, plant uptake efficiency, or nutrient interactions.
WSP uses the source recipe's bone/vinegar steps; the candidate plant material is a derived substitution, not a source recipe.
The crop requirement unit (kg/ha) is confirmed by the owner (2026-10-18) even though Crop_Requirements.json does not state it.
The no-overshoot sizing keeps the target fraction from being exceeded, so nutrients that are not the sizing nutrient are deliberately under-supplied; their coverage and top-up note are reported.

The implied mulch depth approximates the fresh material's loose volume with the approved plant-tea water-to-material convention (10 L water per kg material), an upper bound on the material volume, so the depth check is conservative.

steps.text: Select ripe fruits, preferably those that are locally available and organic.
Chop the fruits into small pieces.
Mix the chopped fruits with brown sugar in a 1:1 ratio by weight.
Place the mixture in a clay pot, plastic jar, or glass jar, leaving some space at the top.
Cover the opening of the jar with a breathable material like a cotton cloth and secure it with a rubber band or thread.
Allow the mixture to ferment in a cool, shaded place for about 7 days.
After fermentation, strain the liquid. This is your FFJ.

interpretation.nutrition_track: The nutrition track is a nutrient-equivalence mass: the stated fresh material, spread as chop-and-drop or mulch or brewed as plant tea, would supply the target fraction of the crop's seasonal N/P/K requirement if the dry-matter and release fractions are correct. The mass is sized by the no-overshoot rule to the nutrient that needs the least, so the target is never exceeded and the other nutrients reach only the stated coverage.
interpretation.booster_track: The booster track is the source recipe at its normal strength. It is a small, convenient input, not a way to cover the crop requirement on the stated area.
interpretation.not_a_prescription: The old 'relative signal, not a dose' caveat is replaced by these explicit assumptions. The output is an assumption-bound calculation, not a fertilizer recommendation or a substitute for soil testing.

limitations: Dry matter is per plant part but every value is a corpus point estimate; bark uses a wood-moisture proxy and flower uses whole-plant water content.
P release uses a plant-uptake efficiency (less than 20%) as a conservative proxy because the corpus has no direct residue-P release measurement.
K release of 0.80 follows 'most of the potassium is leached' rather than a measured fraction.
The plant-tea steep ratio (10 L water per kg fresh material) is a method convention; only the 1:10 finished-tea dilution and the application rate are corpus-sourced.
The ferment density is a water-density unit convention, not a measured extract density.
The model does not account for soil nutrient supply, leaching, volatilization, fixation, plant uptake efficiency, or nutrient interactions.
WSP uses the source recipe's bone/vinegar steps; the candidate plant material is a derived substitution, not a source recipe.
The crop requirement unit (kg/ha) is confirmed by the owner (2026-10-18) even though Crop_Requirements.json does not state it.
The no-overshoot sizing keeps the target fraction from being exceeded, so nutrients that are not the sizing nutrient are deliberately under-supplied; their coverage and top-up note are reported.

The implied mulch depth approximates the fresh material's loose volume with the approved plant-tea water-to-material convention (10 L water per kg material), an upper bound on the material volume, so the depth check is conservative.

steps.text: Select ripe fruits, preferably those that are locally available and organic.
Chop the fruits into small pieces.
Mix the chopped fruits with brown sugar in a 1:1 ratio by weight.
Place the mixture in a clay pot, plastic jar, or glass jar, leaving some space at the top.
Cover the opening of the jar with a breathable material like a cotton cloth and secure it with a rubber band or thread.
Allow the mixture to ferment in a cool, shaded place for about 7 days.
After fermentation, strain the liquid. This is your FFJ.

steps.text: Collect the young shoots of plants early in the morning when the dew is still present.
Chop the shoots into small pieces.
Mix the chopped shoots with brown sugar in a 1:1 ratio by weight.
Place the mixture in a clay pot, plastic jar, or glass jar, leaving some space at the top.
Cover the opening of the jar with a breathable material like a cotton cloth and secure it with a rubber band or thread.
Allow the mixture to ferment in a cool, shaded place for about 7 days.
After fermentation, strain the liquid. This is your FPJ.

track_model.nutrition: Fresh plant material is computed per nutrient from the crop requirement, the candidate tissue midpoint, the tissue part's dry-matter fraction and the nutrient's release fraction. The no-overshoot rule sizes the material to the nutrient that needs the least, so no nutrient exceeds the target fraction; each nutrient's resulting coverage is reported.
track_model.booster: The booster is the source recipe's standard batch at its standard dilution and application rate. Its nutrient amount is reported for information only and does not claim to cover the crop requirement.
track_model.dry_matter: Dry matter is per plant part; the value's corpus source is recorded for each part. Unmapped parts fall back to the herb category.
track_model.release: Release/extraction is per nutrient (N, P, K); the residue-N recovery figure is not reused for P and K.
track_model.dose_rule: no overshoot: the single applied mass is the smallest per-nutrient requirement, so the target fraction is never exceeded; shortfalls are reported as coverage with a top-up note

interpretation.nutrition_track: The nutrition track is a nutrient-equivalence mass: the stated fresh material, spread as chop-and-drop or mulch or brewed as plant tea, would supply the target fraction of the crop's seasonal N/P/K requirement if the dry-matter and release fractions are correct. The mass is sized by the no-overshoot rule to the nutrient that needs the least, so the target is never exceeded and the other nutrients reach only the stated coverage.
interpretation.booster_track: The booster track is the source recipe at its normal strength. It is a small, convenient input, not a way to cover the crop requirement on the stated area.
interpretation.not_a_prescription: The old 'relative signal, not a dose' caveat is replaced by these explicit assumptions. The output is an assumption-bound calculation, not a fertilizer recommendation or a substitute for soil testing.

limitations: Dry matter is per plant part but every value is a corpus point estimate; bark uses a wood-moisture proxy and flower uses whole-plant water content.
P release uses a plant-uptake efficiency (less than 20%) as a conservative proxy because the corpus has no direct residue-P release measurement.
K release of 0.80 follows 'most of the potassium is leached' rather than a measured fraction.
The plant-tea steep ratio (10 L water per kg fresh material) is a method convention; only the 1:10 finished-tea dilution and the application rate are corpus-sourced.
The ferment density is a water-density unit convention, not a measured extract density.
The model does not account for soil nutrient supply, leaching, volatilization, fixation, plant uptake efficiency, or nutrient interactions.
WSP uses the source recipe's bone/vinegar steps; the candidate plant material is a derived substitution, not a source recipe.
The crop requirement unit (kg/ha) is confirmed by the owner (2026-10-18) even though Crop_Requirements.json does not state it.
The no-overshoot sizing keeps the target fraction from being exceeded, so nutrients that are not the sizing nutrient are deliberately under-supplied; their coverage and top-up note are reported.

The implied mulch depth approximates the fresh material's loose volume with the approved plant-tea water-to-material convention (10 L water per kg material), an upper bound on the material volume, so the depth check is conservative.

source.derivation: Midpoint of 1-2 t per 100a; 100a = 1 ha and 1 t = 1000 L.

plant_tea_steep_water_l_per_kg.unit: L water per kg fresh plant material

source.quote: Simply fill an old pillowcase or burlap bag with your chosen material (comfrey, nettles, compost or manure) and sink it into a large bucket or barrel of water.
source.derivation: The corpus says to cover the material with water but gives no numeric material:water ratio. v2 proposes 10 L water per kg fresh material so the tea volume is transparent and testable; this is the one steep-ratio convention in the proposal.

plant_tea_steep_water_l_per_kg.caveat: A method convention proposed for arithmetic transparency, not a corpus measurement. Approved by the owner (2026-10-18).

plant_tea_dilution_ratio.unit: L water per L finished tea concentrate

source.quote: The liquid feed must be diluted before it is applied to plants at a ratio of about 10 parts water to 1 part concentrate.

plant_tea_dilution_ratio.caveat: The corpus recipe is comfrey tea; the same dilution is proposed for a candidate-plant tea. JADAM's JLF standard is a different, much weaker 1:100 dilution.

source.quote: Standard is ×100 dilution. Calculate the volume of liquid fertilizer based on 1 t (264 gal) of water being used for 0.03 ha (0.08 ac).
source.derivation: 1000 L diluted liquid per 0.03 ha = 1000 / 300 m2 = 3.333 L/m2.

plant_tea_application_rate_l_per_m2.caveat: The quote is JADAM liquid fertilizer at its standard 1:100 dilution, not the 1:10 comfrey tea. v2 uses it only to say whether the full-requirement tea volume fits a normal liquid application.

source.quote: Grass clippings are a cheap, effective mulch. Apply them at a maximum depth of 5cm (2in) or the heat they create as they decompose may harm the stems.

mulch_depth_cm.caveat: The 5 cm maximum is for grass clippings; coarser or drier materials can be applied deeper (the corpus also describes 8-12 inch sheet mulch). v2 reports it as the default fresh-material mulch depth.

source.quote: Matches the existing bioaccumulator_oracle.py ratio rounding.
Six decimals keeps small standard-rate batches visible while staying stable across Python and Dart double arithmetic.

track_model.nutrition: Fresh plant material is computed per nutrient from the crop requirement, the candidate tissue midpoint, the tissue part's dry-matter fraction and the nutrient's release fraction. The no-overshoot rule sizes the material to the nutrient that needs the least, so no nutrient exceeds the target fraction; each nutrient's resulting coverage is reported.
track_model.booster: The booster is the source recipe's standard batch at its standard dilution and application rate. Its nutrient amount is reported for information only and does not claim to cover the crop requirement.
track_model.dry_matter: Dry matter is per plant part; the value's corpus source is recorded for each part. Unmapped parts fall back to the herb category.
track_model.release: Release/extraction is per nutrient (N, P, K); the residue-N recovery figure is not reused for P and K.
track_model.dose_rule: no overshoot: the single applied mass is the smallest per-nutrient requirement, so the target fraction is never exceeded; shortfalls are reported as coverage with a top-up note

candidate_policy.order: each recipe offers its recipe-named plants first, then the top catalog plants by tissue content for the recipe's nutrient

interpretation.nutrition_track: The nutrition track is a nutrient-equivalence mass: the stated fresh material, spread as chop-and-drop or mulch or brewed as plant tea, would supply the target fraction of the crop's seasonal N/P/K requirement if the dry-matter and release fractions are correct. The mass is sized by the no-overshoot rule to the nutrient that needs the least, so the target is never exceeded and the other nutrients reach only the stated coverage.
interpretation.booster_track: The booster track is the source recipe at its normal strength. It is a small, convenient input, not a way to cover the crop requirement on the stated area.
interpretation.not_a_prescription: The old 'relative signal, not a dose' caveat is replaced by these explicit assumptions. The output is an assumption-bound calculation, not a fertilizer recommendation or a substitute for soil testing.

limitations: Dry matter is per plant part but every value is a corpus point estimate; bark uses a wood-moisture proxy and flower uses whole-plant water content.
P release uses a plant-uptake efficiency (less than 20%) as a conservative proxy because the corpus has no direct residue-P release measurement.
K release of 0.80 follows 'most of the potassium is leached' rather than a measured fraction.
The plant-tea steep ratio (10 L water per kg fresh material) is a method convention; only the 1:10 finished-tea dilution and the application rate are corpus-sourced.
The ferment density is a water-density unit convention, not a measured extract density.
The model does not account for soil nutrient supply, leaching, volatilization, fixation, plant uptake efficiency, or nutrient interactions.
WSP uses the source recipe's bone/vinegar steps; the candidate plant material is a derived substitution, not a source recipe.
The crop requirement unit (kg/ha) is confirmed by the owner (2026-10-18) even though Crop_Requirements.json does not state it.
The no-overshoot sizing keeps the target fraction from being exceeded, so nutrients that are not the sizing nutrient are deliberately under-supplied; their coverage and top-up note are reported.

The implied mulch depth approximates the fresh material's loose volume with the approved plant-tea water-to-material convention (10 L water per kg material), an upper bound on the material volume, so the depth check is conservative.
